title: Turkish police detain dozens in raids on gay bars and homes of LGBTQ+ activists
description: Police in Turkey have detained 47 people in a series of raids on gay bars and the homes of LGBTQ+ activists, officials say.Raids took place in 12 prov
body: Police in Turkey have detained 47 people in a series of raids on gay bars and the homes of LGBTQ+ activists, officials say.Raids took place in 12 provinces over the weekend as part of a campaign dubbed "My Family is Safe" that the Turkish government says has been designed to protect family values. One of the targets of the operation was LGBTQ+ association Kaos GL. Same-sex marriage is not recognised in Turkey, with growing pressure on gay couples. Human rights groups in Turkey have accused the government of using the campaign to target the LGBTQ+ community. Officers detained 26 people and seized drugs, digital equipment, smuggled alcohol and a firearm during the raids, according to the Istanbul chief prosecutor's office. In a separate statement, the Ankara chief prosecutor's office said another 21 people had been detained as part of an investigation into Kaos GL. The organisation said 50 activists had been detained, more than 10 taken after police raids on their homes.It said that authorities had blocked several websites and social media accounts linked to LGBTQ+ organisations.According to the group, authorities have accused Kaos GL of making "obscenity" in online posts that are available to children and had demanded the shutting down of the Kaos GL X account, as well as those of around 15 other LGBTQ+ organisations.Same-sex relations are not an offence in Turkey but homophobia is common, with President Recep Tayyip Erdogan describing LGBTQ people as "perverts" responsible for the falling birth rate.As part of "My Family is Safe", Turkish Justice Minister Akin Gurlek says legal proceedings have been started against more than 160 people and a number of organisations and companies across the country. Gurlek did not say how many people had been taken into custody, but said the raids came in the context of the "Decade of the Family" campaign.However, the Turkish Human Rights Association says the Turkish government has been using the campaign to target the LGBTQ+ community in recent years. "The real name of this operation is not 'My Family is Safe'; it is state-led discrimination, politics of fear and the dismantling of civil society," the organisation said on X.

schema.headline: Turkish police detain dozens in raids on gay bars and homes of LGBTQ+ activists

title: Spanish Grand Prix result: Kimi Antonelli wins after Lando Norris loses lead because of virtual safety car timing
description: Mercedes driver Kimi Antonelli won the Spanish Grand Prix after McLaren's Lando Norris lost out because of the bad timing of a virtual safety car.Norr
body: Mercedes driver Kimi Antonelli won the Spanish Grand Prix after McLaren's Lando Norris lost out because of the bad timing of a virtual safety car.Norris was leading comfortably from pole position when the VSC was called on lap 15. The timing was terrible for the world champion - he had already passed the pit exit when the VSC was called.That meant Antonelli and Verstappen were able to pit under the VSC, saving time, while the caution period ended before Norris could make it around to the pits again.He did then come in but, to make matters worse, the stop was slow and he rejoined in fifth place.Norris was able to recover only to third around this track where overtaking is next to impossible.Antonelli's eighth win in 14 races this year puts an even tighter stranglehold on the championship for the Italian.He is now 81 points ahead of team-mate George Russell, who finished fifth after a difficult race on a confusing strategy, and 101 clear of Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton, who retired early on with brake failure."It's good to win but it doesn't feel as good because Lando deserved to win," Antonelli said.Norris said: "We'll take it on the chin. There could be more wins this year."The key stories of the maiden race on the new Madring were:Norris' terrible luck with the VSC depriving him of a likely third victory this year after a brilliant pole on SaturdayAntonelli's fortune in a season that is surrendering to him as well as him grabbing it by the throat with his performancesThe difficulty of overtaking on a new track designed from a clean sheet of paper, yet without obvious overtaking placesNorris knew that holding on to the lead would be tough from pole but he robustly defended from Antonelli into the first corner.The Mercedes driver cut the chicanes at Turns One and Two, and again at Turns Five and Six, each time getting into the lead, each time having to give it back.After that, Norris set about building a lead and looked to be in control of the race   as he extended his lead progressively, moving 5.6 seconds clear 10 laps in, and 6.2 when Lance Stroll's Aston Martin stopped at Turn 20 with brake failure.The VSC was called, but Norris had already reached the pit straight, while Antonelli and Red Bull's Max Verstappen had not and could come in.Norris came in the next time around, but the VSC ended a couple of corners before he reached the entry to the pits, allowing the cars still on track to get back up to racing speed - a stop under a safety car saves a driver about 10 seconds over one under green-flag conditions.To make matters worse, McLaren's mechanics had trouble with both the right-hand side wheels, and the stop took seven seconds rather than the usual two.Norris came out in fifth place, 6.3secs behind Russell, and his hopes of winning were gone.At the front, Ferrari's Charles Leclerc, who had been running fourth before the VSC, stayed out, having started the race on hard tyres rather than the mediums chosen by Antonelli and Norris and the softs Verstappen had.Leclerc stayed out, and led the race with Antonelli close behind but the gap fluctuating as the Mercedes driver managed his tyres.Ferrari kept Leclerc out as long as possible, hoping for a second safety car to enable him to make his own cheap stop.But one never came, and Leclerc had to pit eventually, on lap 48 with nine to go. He resumed in fourth behind Antonelli, Verstappen and Norris.Norris had closed all his deficit to Verstappen by the final stages and was running right on the Dutchman's tail in the closing laps, but was unable to pass.The closest he came was with two laps to go as Verstappen stumbled over some lapped cars, but despite a mistake at Turn Five, the Dutchman was able to hold on.Officials briefly looked at an incident with two laps to go when he cut a chicane while fighting to stay ahead of Norris, who complained Verstappen should give the place up. But no action was taken.Russell ended up a lonely fifth after starting on the hard tyres and then moving on to a mystifying strategy that saw him switch to medium tyres at the VSC and then have to stop again for hards at about half distance.He spent much of the race debating strategy with his team before being told to be quiet and they would debate it afterwards.Red Bull's Liam Lawson took sixth, ahead of Alpine's Frano Colapinto, McLaren's Oscar Piastri, delayed by a front wing issue after colliding with Russell on the first lap.Racing Bulls' Arvid Lindblad took ninth place from Audi's Nico Hulkenberg with two laps to go.The drivers had warned that overtaking would be almost impossible, and so it proved.The pressure that was already there to rethink the layout for next year and provide a longer straight and big braking zone to allow overtaking will be significant.Rethinking the fractured and overly extensive breadth of the paddock and pits complex - which covers a vastly greater distance than anywhere else - would also be a good idea.

schema.headline: Spanish Grand Prix result: Kimi Antonelli wins after Lando Norris loses lead because of virtual safety car timing

title: Reform's £72m donations 'entirely in line with law', Jenrick says
description: Robert Jenrick has said Reform UK believed that £72m in donations it has received from two cryptocurrency billionaires were "entirely in line with the
body: Robert Jenrick has said Reform UK believed that £72m in donations it has received from two cryptocurrency billionaires were "entirely in line with the law".The party's economic spokesman told the BBC that he did not expect that it will have to return any of the money from Ben Delo and Christopher Harborne, who are both British and have spent time living overseas.The government is seeking to change the law on donations to UK political parties from British expats, including a £100,000 cap backdated to 25 March."These two donations are entirely in line with the law as it is and, as far as we know, the law as it's going to be in the future," Jenrick said.As well as limiting how much British citizens can donate to political parties from overseas, the government has proposed a minimum residency period in which the £100,000 cap would still apply for those who move back to the UK.This would be in place for the remainder of the calendar year and the following calendar year after the person returns.Housing Secretary Angela Rayner told the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg that the rule changes would apply retrospectively and anyone not complying with them would have "to return that money".Rayner added she was not commenting specifically on Delo and Harborne as she does not "understand" their "circumstances". Answering questions about the donations following Rayner's remarks, Jenrick said: "It might be that Angela Rayner or the government keep trying to change the law to make it even harder for people to donate to Reform, nothing would surprise me. "But, as it stands, we believe these are entirely in line with the law."BBC News has been told that both Delo and Harborne have returned to the UK. Delo is understood to have been back in the country since last year.Jenrick said Delo had returned to the UK "in part so that he can comply with the changes to the law".In a statement after the programme, a Reform UK spokesman said: "We are 100% confident both [donations] are legal and won't ever have to handed back."One person familiar with the government's proposed changes said the issue of whether Delo and Harborne are affected would likely come down to how ministers choose to define UK residency.They said one way would be to adopt the same definition used in tax laws, but stressed how complex the rules around residency are.The government's proposed changes were added to the Representation of the People Bill after they were approved by MPs this month. The bill still needs to be scrutinised in the House of Lords.Rayner said the proposals were "directly as a result" of a review by former top civil servant Philip Rycroft, external, published on 25 March.Rayner said: "We said that because of the intention of the legislation and the recommendations, which we accepted, was known in the public domain that it would be retrospective to that date."That legislation is going through Parliament at the moment and we've also written to the Electoral Commission, which is an independent body, to see what further measures we need to take to protect our democracy."There are currently no restrictions on the amount of money UK-based donors can give to political parties.The government has previously said it was "determined to tackle" the issue of "mega-donors", and has established a new taskforce to do this.It did not support calls from some MPs for a cap but Rayner left the door open to the possibility of further restrictions."It's not as simple as we're saying we won't put a cap [on donations], it's a question of making sure that the task and finish group look at how we implement this."Rayner said the aim would be to "protect our democracy in the spirit of individuals not being able to overpower and buy their way into democracy at the expense of those people that are at the ballot box".Conservative shadow foreign secretary Tom Tugendhat said it was important to ensure "we do not end up with a sort of Americanisation of politics where money just sort of runs free".He said people should be able to support the democratic movements they wished but added that "what we've got to be careful about is where different industries, where different financial sources raise questions".Liberal Democrat Cabinet Office spokeswoman Lisa Smart said there should be emergency legislation to cap campaign donations and spending.She said: "No politician should be able to buy the keys to Number 10."A Green Party spokesperson said there needed to be "more robust laws" around political donations, adding: "The Labour Party urgently needs to find its spine and support a tight cap on donations from individuals."Jenrick said Delo and Harborne  - who each gave £36m to the party in two days and now share the record for the largest ever donation given to a UK political party - were "not buying anything, they simply support our agenda".Both men had already donated millions of pounds to Reform ahead of the announcement of their latest contributions.The Times reported in June that Harborne, who has been based in Thailand, had registered to vote in the UK, while Delo had told the Telegraph in April that he was moving back from Hong Kong.Harborne wrote in the Telegraph on Saturday that Reform was a "start-up party" that lacked "the benefit of hundreds of years of patronage". Delo had written in the newspaper the day prior that he wanted to enable Reform to put up a "fair fight at the next election.The £72m from the two is more than the total received by all UK political parties last year.Delo was pardoned by US President Donald Trump last year over a breach of anti-money laundering laws at his crypto trading platform, BitMex, to which he had pleaded guilty in 2022.Reform's fundraising has come under scrutiny in recent months. This includes police announcing an investigation over allegations the party broke foreign funding laws in a broadcast by Channel 4 News last week.The party's leader Nigel Farage is also under investigation by the parliamentary standards commissioner over whether he should have declared a £5m gift he received from Harborne ahead of the 2024 election.Both Reform and Farage have denied any wrongdoing in both instances.

schema.headline: Reform's £72m donations 'entirely in line with law', Jenrick says

title: AI staff 'genuinely frightened' for humanity's future, ex-Anthropic researcher tells BBC
description: An artificial intelligence researcher who quit AI firm Anthropic has said people working on the technology were "genuinely frightened" about the speed
body: An artificial intelligence researcher who quit AI firm Anthropic has said people working on the technology were "genuinely frightened" about the speed of its advancements and what it could mean for humanity."I believe that if we don't slow down at the current rate of progress, there is a strong chance that we could all die in the immediate future," he said.Jacob Coxon was speaking to the BBC after his resignation post on the dangers of AI went viral on a backdrop of growing safety concerns about the industry. The 27-year-old's former boss, Anthropic head Dario Amodei, recently called for AI development to slow down - though some have questioned the motivations behind this.The bosses of two rival AI firms, Sam Altman of OpenAI and Elon Musk of xAI, have both said they agree with Amodei's proposal for industry-wide deceleration and regulation, as well as independent monitoring of AI model development.Amodei wrote in an essay on Saturday that developing the technology was not in question, but the risks associated with it were "serious", and that companies and governments must be given time to address them.Coxon – who worked at OpenAI before joining Anthropic – welcomed the suggestion of a slowdown but said it would need to be co-ordinated with China to avoid "a race at an international scale"."The people who work at these companies are completely serious when they ask for regulation because they find themselves trapped in a race. And they're scared of the outcomes of that race," he told Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg.The hardest question to answer, according to Coxon, was what an AI apocalypse would look like.One of the risks outlined in Amodei's comments was of a swarm of bots acting like a supercomputer that could take over the internet.Coxon said this scenario could be realistic in six months to a year.In response to Coxon's departure, an Anthropic spokesperson told BBC News: "We have always been transparent that AI will bring both enormous benefits and unprecedented risks."To address these risks, we continue to build models with some of the strongest safeguards in the industry."The firm has been a pioneer in studying how AI models work, the spokesperson added. It was the first to publish a framework for mitigating the risks posed by their development - and it also "aggressively" tests its models and publishes the findings to aid scrutiny and prevent incidents of "AI misalignment"."This work is also why we believe the world would benefit from the industry adopting a lawful, verifiable way to work together to pace how we release powerful models," they said.Coxon said his peers feared the danger could even arrive in the next two years. He said staff at AI firms were "planning what to do with their lives and thinking about the impacts of their work", while some were "considering buying land somewhere because they're so scared of the instability as a result of rapid AI progress". "They all keep this in their head on a daily basis while working on the technology."But Coxon did have some optimism about the future of AI, telling the BBC that the people researching the technology "genuinely want to see the upside" of things like "solving diseases and improving everyone's lives".However, some industry figures have suggested comments are overstated or may be designed to generate hype.Chief executive of the AI platform Hugging Face, Clement Delangue, said on social media: "Sorry, but asking Jacob [Coxon] about AI extinction risk is like asking your AC guy about climate change. Not saying it's necessarily uninteresting or wrong per se but let's keep things in perspective."After Amodei's essay was published, however, Delangue offered to help be a part of the potential solutions the Anthropic boss proposed.Grindr chief executive George Arison expressed similar views when talking to the BBC, suggesting Anthropic and others statements were being made to drum up investor support."Because the only way to justify these valuations is to actually claim: 'I'm going to take over every industry and I'm going to take over every job, and my AI is going to be doing all that work,'" he said.Jensen Huang, boss on AI chip maker Nvdia, also discussed Coxon's comments at a conference hosted by the investment bank Goldman Sachs last week, multiple people in the group told the BBC. They said he dismissed them as untrue.Meanwhile, US President Donald Trump told reporters on Sunday that the US was "leading China in AI... And frankly, I want to keep it that way. Because whoever wins AI wins".Other critics say Anthropic has been trying to trigger a regulatory push to block competition, leaving it and OpenAI in a duopoly.Anthropic is reportedly preparing for a potentially record-setting initial public offering on the stock market, allowing people to buy shares in its firm. OpenAI, which was most recently valued at $852bn (£630bn), had been expected to do the same, but OpenAI's Altman said on Friday this would not happen this year, citing AI safety concerns.

schema.headline: AI staff 'genuinely frightened' for humanity's future, ex-Anthropic researcher tells BBC

title: Trump: US president doubles down on united Ireland comments on day two of visit
description: Image source, PA MediaImage caption, Donald Trump is on day two of the visit to Ireland where he will spend the day at Trump International Golf Links
body: Image source, PA MediaImage caption, Donald Trump is on day two of the visit to Ireland where he will spend the day at Trump International Golf Links in Doonbeg, County Clare, for the Irish OpenByEnda McClafferty and Niall McCrackenin Doonbeg, County ClareUpdated 1 hour agoPresident Donald Trump has doubled down on his support for a united Ireland.He's on day two of a visit, which he is spending at Trump International Golf Links in Doonbeg, County Clare, for the Irish Open.On Saturday, Trump told reporters he would love to see a united Ireland while at a meeting with the Taoiseach (Irish PM) Micheál Martin in Dublin.Speaking on Sunday at his Doonbeg golf resort, he said it would be natural to put Ireland and Northern Ireland "together". He spoke to reporters after watching the tournament leader Irish golfer Shane Lowry tee off.He described what he said about a united Ireland as "a fairly routine comment"."I've always loved the people of Ireland. It just seems to me you have Northern Ireland and Ireland," he said"It seems that one of the naturals of all time is to put them together."That's only my opinion, and by the way many people agree."The president sidestepped a question about Scottish independence."I won't talk about Scotland yet I will save that," he said.A major security operation is continuing for Trump's visit to Ireland.He will leave from Shannon Airport on Sunday evening.The taoiseach is also attending the concluding stages of the Irish Open, where he met Trump again.Protests continue against Trump visitMore than 10,000 people marched through Dublin on Saturday to show their opposition to the US president.Others protesting against the visit have been arriving in buses to Doonbeg on Sunday, with about 100 protesters present.A small crowd were moved from the president's hotel by Gardai (Irish police), Irish broadcaster RTÉ is reporting.On Saturday evening, three women were arrested for trespassing on the golf links at Doonbeg and appeared at a special sitting of Ennis District Court.Rev Steven Foster, a Methodist minister from Galway, attended the anti-Trump protest in Doonbeg. "I'm here because Trump is the exact opposite of everything I stand for as a follower of Jesus," he told BBC News NI.Image caption, Rev Steven Foster is in Doonbeg to protest against the visit Foster added: "As a church leader, it's important for me to be visible, and the church needs to be visible in this regard."Foster said the "type of welcome he has been given sends out a terrible message". Golf course is a 'massive employer'Image caption, Martin Kelly, who's a business owner, says the golf course is a "massive business" for DoonbegHowever, others have praised Trump for the benefits and jobs his golf course brings to the local area.Martin Kelly is a local businessman from Doonbeg and said the village is "very fortunate" to have the Trump International Golf Course."It's a massive employer here to be honest with you," he told BBC News NI."There's nothing else about here at that scale; they're very decent people to work for, they're very fair."He said local people are "very proud" that the golf tournament is taking place there. "We're not into politics here, we're into business. And it's a massive business to us. Doonbeg is one of the best links course in the world. Donald Trump isn't perfect but look he's not doing a bad job either."Hopefully Shane Lowry can win now with the help of God, and hopefully he can come to Doonbeg afterwards for a beer, I'll buy him one if he does."Image caption, Publican Seoirse Comerford says the golf course gives "a big boost" to the local economy Seoirse Comerford owns the Comerford bar in Doonbeg. He described the tournament as "unbelievable"."If you look at the red double decker buses going up and down the street full of people, we never thought we would have seen the like of that."He said the golf course is a big employer and is keeping Doonbeg "alive". "Most rural villages in west Clare are all dying a death, young people going away to college, they don't come back."Like there's over 300 people employed up there at the golf course , it's a big boost to the local economy.  You've got big companies in Dublin, like Intel, the golf course is our Intel down here."I probably wouldn't have taken over the bar business other than the golf course being up there. "We would have had 1,000 plus through the pub on Saturday night and the same Friday night, so there's a lot of people around the village, which is great to see."

schema.headline: Trump: US president doubles down on united Ireland comments on day two of visit

title: Brics summit 2026 Delhi: Iran war reshapes ties but exposes divides
description: This weekend, some of the most powerful people in the world gathered in Delhi around a vast circular table.Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi announc
body: This weekend, some of the most powerful people in the world gathered in Delhi around a vast circular table.Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi announced that together, the leaders next to him should increasingly become "rule-shapers", not "rule-takers".Among those listening were members of the Brics group, including Chinese President Xi Jinping, Russian President Vladimir Putin, Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian, Abu Dhabi's Crown Prince Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan and South African President Cyril Ramaphosa.These are hardly natural allies. They have histories of border disputes and even military confrontations.India and China engaged in a deadly clash along their disputed border in 2020. Iran and the UAE have been on opposing ends of the war in the Middle East, with Tehran launching missiles and drones at its fellow Brics member as the conflict sent shockwaves across global economies.The fact that India was able to gather these leaders together in person is a feat in and of itself and testament to its diplomatic reach. The weekend also provided a platform for countries to reassess their relationships in light of the Iran war.But agreeing on what a new global order should look like and achieving clear, tangible outcomes was a much harder task, and that tension ran through this weekend's summit.The summit succeeded in delivering a joint declaration when divisions among members have rarely been so glaring.Twice earlier this year, meetings between Brics ministers had failed to produce a joint statement. This time a consensus was reached, but by side-stepping issues that members sharply disagree on, with few solutions.The "New Delhi Declaration" was adopted on the first day of the summit. But what is striking is what it doesn't say.On the war in the Middle East, the declaration urges "maximum restraint". It also condemns "attacks on civilian infrastructure and peaceful nuclear facilities" but assigns no blame.It reiterates support for a two-state solution, opposes forced displacement of Palestinians or actions that could "legitimise or prolong occupation", framing it carefully around existing UN resolutions.It makes no mention at all of Russia's war in Ukraine, a departure from previous Brics declarations.There is similar caution on trade. It lists concerns over "indiscriminate rising tariffs" and condemns unilateral sanctions but stops short of naming the US, and is likely to avoid Washington's ire.Trump shadow looms large over Brics as Modi hosts Putin and Xi in DelhiSeveral Brics members would have been loath to draw President Donald Trump's anger, as he has previously called the group's proposals, including potentially linking central-bank digital currencies for cross-border trade, "anti-American"."Not mentioning any country by name, even as they condemned the conflict in the Middle East, bears the hallmark of India," says Praveen Donthi, senior analyst at the International Crisis Group."I was pleasantly surprised that there was a strong reference to tariffs, because India could have wanted to be less direct about it, but perhaps this was a chance to convey their displeasure," he added.In the wake of Trump's trade threats and the shock of the war in the Middle East, reshaping the global order has become a vital need for many member economies.What the summit did provide is a platform for meetings that seemed hard to imagine just a few months ago.Iran's Pezeshkian and Abu Dhabi's Crown Prince sat down for talks together - the highest-level face-to-face meeting known between the two countries since the war began.This weekend offered Tehran a chance to show that it does not stand alone amid the US and Israel's military attacks and economic pressure.As Iran tries to withstand US sanctions, Washington's "Operation Economic Outcast" and a naval blockade on its ports, Pezeshkian pressed for deeper economic ties with Brics members, including Malaysia, India and Ethiopia.As for China, this was President Xi's first visit to Delhi in seven years. There has been deep mistrust between China and India since the 2020 border dispute, but those tensions have eased. There is also a large trade imbalance, with a deficit tilting heavily in China's favour.There was a cordial handshake between Xi and Modi, not the latter's signature hug. Xi also stayed for less than 24 hours, skipping the gala dinner hosted by Modi on Saturday night.But the weekend was still a big moment for two countries with such a difficult relationship. According to official readouts, the two leaders agreed to strengthen business ties and transport links and address barriers to trade.Trigunayat believes this is part of a gradual warming of relations in recent years, and that there is a will on both sides to work together. But whether it will produce substantial progress remains to be seen."I always say we have to trust, but verify first," he says.

schema.headline: Brics summit 2026 Delhi: Iran war reshapes ties but exposes divides

title: Tom Felton: I'm so excited to see Rupert Grint play Ron Weasley again
description: Image source, Getty ImagesByYasmin RufoCulture reporterReporting fromin New YorkEvery night on Broadway, Tom Felton walks on stage to a roar from the
body: Image source, Getty ImagesByYasmin RufoCulture reporterReporting fromin New YorkEvery night on Broadway, Tom Felton walks on stage to a roar from the audience. He had expected the reaction to die down after the first week, but it never did.Almost 15 years after his final appearance as Draco Malfoy on screen, Felton has spent the past 10 months playing the character again in the Broadway production of Harry Potter and the Cursed Child.I meet the actor in a dressing room at NBC Studios, just off Times Square in New York. He's just finished a live television appearance and in a few hours will be back on stage for his next performance.He greets me with a hug and says he is excited to speak to BBC News because his mum and 100-year-old grandfather will see it. His family are some of his biggest supporters - his mum has seen the show five times already, while his dad is due to visit next month.That support mirrors the enthusiasm Felton has encountered from Harry Potter fans, which he says still surprises him more than two decades after he first played Draco."I thought the applause would stop in the first week and it has not."It's very humbling and lovely to know how much the characters still mean to people now and if it brings them to the theatre, that's the best."He is also struck by how many of the fans now approaching him were not alive when the first Harry Potter film was released."There are fans that approach me shouting 'Draco' who weren't even born when I was in the first film," he says.Image source, Warner Bros. Pictures & Manuel HarlanFelton was the first of the original Harry Potter cast to reprise his role in the theatre show, but he will not be the only one for much longer, as Rupert Grint is set to return as Ron Weasley on Broadway in February.The 38-year-old actor says he called his former co-star as soon as he heard the news."We are typically - and he will agree with me - pretty bad at our phone game, but when I heard the news I called him immediately and I'm so excited for him," Felton says. "Who doesn't want to see Rupert Grint play Ron Weasley again? Come on!"I ask whether Felton offered any advice to his co-star but he laughs and says absolutely not, pointing out that Grint has already appeared on Broadway."I don't think he needs any advice from me. If anything, I would be taking it from him."He adds that Grint has a "Ron Weasley laissez-faire approach to these things".More than two decades after they first met on the Harry Potter set, Felton says the friendships between the young cast have endured.He describes Grint, Daniel Radcliffe and Emma Watson as "best mates" and "family", even if getting them all in the same place is now difficult."We are usually in four different corners of the Earth, so it's hard to get together," he says, adding that their support since his return to Draco has been "fantastic".Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Daniel Radcliffe, Emma Watson, Rupert Grint and Tom Felton are pictured in 2010 at the premiere of Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows - Part 1As Felton and Grint return to familiar roles on stage, a new generation is preparing to take over the characters in HBO's television adaptation of the books set to air later this year.Felton recently met his successor, Lox Pratt, and "saw a lot of myself in him".Felton says he was struck by Pratt's confidence and describes him as a "charming young man and fabulous actor".Their families have even been in touch."My mum is in contact with his mum and I'm encouraging him to be as cheeky as possible - but professional first."Felton says he is not worried about the level of scrutiny Pratt and the other young actors may face as they take on some of the best-known characters in popular culture."You just enjoy it for what it is."I'm not worried about that at all for him. He's got a very good head on his shoulders and what you don't know doesn't hurt you. I'm sure he's not one to scroll through negative comments."'Dive deeper into Draco'Nor does Felton appear concerned that Harry Potter is being adapted again relatively soon after the films.Instead, he says the longer television format offers the chance to explore parts of the books that the films did not have time for."We had two hours to fit in a lot of content and the wizarding world is vast, so it's exciting to know they can dive in deeper.""I hope the fans of the books and films explore more about Draco," he says.While some actors might want to distance themselves from the role that made them famous, Felton has embraced his connection to Harry Potter.He says the franchise has given him "a life I could never have imagined" and that, even today, it is "bringing people together from every corner of the earth".Asked whether this really is the last time he will play Draco, Felton is reluctant to rule anything out."I suppose I said 15 years ago that was the end of Draco and I was leaving him forever, but here I am."It's hard to say with any certainty what's to come."

schema.headline: Tom Felton: I'm so excited to see Rupert Grint play Ron Weasley again

title: They lost their jobs after posting about Charlie Kirk, but some have no regrets
description: In September 2025, Gerald Bourguet felt he was finally living his dream life: he and his wife had bought a house with a pool, they had just welcomed a
body: In September 2025, Gerald Bourguet felt he was finally living his dream life: he and his wife had bought a house with a pool, they had just welcomed a baby boy, and he was writing about professional men's basketball as his full-time job.But all of that changed after he made a series of online posts critical of the late conservative activist Charlie Kirk hours after he was fatally shot on 10 September, while speaking on the campus of Utah Valley University.In the posts, Bourguet described Kirk as an "evil man" and suggested he had dedicated his life to hateful causes. He also criticised Kirk's supporters saying they had not been vocal about school shootings."I had seen the way that people were talking about this person - kind of eulogising him and lionising him and it bothered me based on a lot of the things that he had said," Bourguet told the BBC.Kirk, who founded Christian youth organisation Turning Point USA, was a divisive figure in US politics. For many on the political right, he was charismatic and had a unique skill in making conservative ideas appeal to young people. But for his opponents, his comments on a large swathe of issues from race to immigration, gun control and gender identity were deeply offensive.Screenshots of Bourguet's critical posts went viral quickly. He was fired from his job, his address was exposed online, and he began receiving threatening text messages, he said. Concerned for their safety, the family fled the state with their four-month-old. They returned months later to sell the house and permanently relocated.A year later, he says he doesn't regret what he said, but acknowledged: "My life will never be the same after this". "At age 35, I am having to start over in a lot of respects… I wouldn't wish this on my worst enemy," Bourguet said from his new location, which the BBC agreed not to disclose.PHNX Sports, Bourguet's former employer, did not respond to the BBC's request for comment.Bourguet was one of hundreds fired or disciplined over critical comments of Kirk after his death. While some of those who have lost their jobs have been reinstated or received restitution - sometimes in the millions - others like Bourguet have had to rebuild from scratch.In the aftermath of Kirk's assassination, most people kept their feelings to themselves, or shared them with close friends.But on polarised social media, people rushed to laud, or denounce, the controversial activist. Some called the criticisms, posted hours after his death, tasteless. But others called for swift action, arguing they were callous, mocking, and could even incite further violence.Laura Loomer, an influential right-wing commentator with nearly 2 million followers on X, warned Kirk's critics to "prepare to have your whole future professional aspirations ruined". The push for punishment also came from the highest levels of US government."When you see someone celebrating Charlie's murder, call them out," Vice-President JD Vance said days after the assassination. "And hell, call their employer," he added.White House spokesperson Davis Ingle told the BBC: "Anyone who engages in or endorses political violence or assassination culture must be condemned in the harshest terms possible."Critics on the left said there was a difference between criticism of Kirk and celebrating his death. Some accused these conservative leaders of hypocrisy, as many had previously bemoaned the rise of "cancel culture" – where people who voice controversial opinions face severe consequences at work and socially."Cancel culture can be good, it's bad when it's applied in the wrong ways," Jordan Pace, a Republican member of the South Carolina House of Representatives, told the BBC. "If you are someone who celebrates political assassinations and the murder of an innocent man with two young children in a way that many people did, then yeah, that's an appropriate way for society to function, to shame those people."Pace had previously called for defunding universities in his state if they didn't take actions against employees who made comments about Kirk. One of his posts was re-shared by US President Donald Trump.Across the nation, some employers – private and public – acted swiftly to the pressure campaign. Reliable figures on the number of people fired or disciplined are hard to come by, but a Reuters tally last November found more than 600 instances. It is likely an under-count because not all cases received national or local press attention.The specific actions that led to these disciplinary decisions run the gamut. In Tennessee, anthropology professor Tamar Shirinian was suspended and later fired for a Facebook comment saying "the world is better off" without Kirk.A Delta Air Lines flight attendant was fired after posting "good riddance" in response to Kirk's killing. Office Depot supply store fired an employee for refusing to serve a customer who had wanted to print flyers for a Kirk vigil. Delta Air Lines declined to comment. Office Depot did not respond to a request for comment.Others were disciplined even if they did not make any direct comments about Kirk or his death. Darren Michael, a theatre professor in Tennessee, was fired after he posted a screenshot of a news article from 2023, that covered Kirk's controversial speech on gun control. In the article, Kirk is quoted saying protecting citizens' rights to own guns was worth it even if it led to some gun deaths every year.Florida's Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission fired biologist Brittney Brown after she reposted a meme that also satirised Kirk's position on gun violence in light of his own shooting."I was absolutely gutted," Brown said about her firing to the BBC. "It was like the entire world just completely flipped on its head in a moment."In the year since Kirk's killing, dozens of lawsuits have been filed across the country by people fired for their comments about the activist, arguing their terminations violated their rights to free speech. The suits have led to substantial pay outs in some cases.Brown agreed to a $485,000 (£355,000) financial settlement – about 12 times Brown's annual salary. Darren Michael was reinstated by the Austin Peay State University and in January, the school agreed to pay him $500,000 to settle legal claims. The school did not respond to a request for comment.In the largest settlement reviewed by the BBC, the University of Tennessee agreed to pay $1.9m to resolve a lawsuit brought by anthropologist Tamar Shirinian, over her "better off" comment. As part of the settlement, she will not be reinstated and has agreed not to reapply for future positions at the school.Recently, an arbitrator ordered The Washington Post to rehire, with back pay, opinion journalist Karen Attiah, who was fired for her online posts that said in part she was not going to engage in "performative mourning for a white man that espoused violence".Several other lawsuits remain pending, the BBC found.Most of the legal actions have been pursued by employees of government institutions, or unionised workers, who have some free-speech protections.But in the US, most private sector employees work under "at-will" contracts, which means they can be can be fired without reason.Even those who have scored some victories don't see it as a win."All I wanted was my job back," biologist Brown said. "How much taxpayer money did they waste on this when I barely made $40,000 a year? So no, it does not feel like justice."Shirinian told the BBC she too had wanted to return to her job but felt a legal case could be a lengthy affair."I took a settlement because this allows me to move on with my life," she told the BBC. "The one small regret that I have is that I will not see my day in court and justice will not be served in that way. But I think that the number of the settlement actually speaks to that anyway."The University of Tennessee and Florida's Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission did not respond to the BBC's request for comment. As an at-will employee at a private company, Bourguet is unlikely to prevail in a lawsuit challenging his dismissal. A year on, he said he has struggled to find work. The new state he lives in has a professional basketball team, but he believes the ordeal has made him unemployable in the small world of sports writers. Instead, he's started his own podcast, although he doubts he can earn enough through it to pay the bills."I have accepted that that life is over and that I need to start a new one." Leaving the country is now on the table, he said.Despite the huge personal and professional costs, those who spoke to the BBC said after months of reflection, they did not regret their actions."I have a right to say what I want to say," Brown said. "They are the ones who should have the regrets, not me," she said referring to her former employer.Shirinian apologised to the university days after her suspension. She told the BBC her comment was "an emotional outburst" that was not intended to be public and that she regretted the tone used."I don't regret the sentiment, however" she said, adding "the sentiment was that I am not sad. And I refuse to be made to feel like I have to be sad that someone who was so hateful was killed".Bourguet also said he does not regret his comments although he has conflicting thoughts about its consequences."I don't regret that line of thinking because I think it's important to push back on things that are steeped in hatred," he said, referring to Kirk's political message. "I don't regret what I said. I don't regret the way that I said it. I do regret the ripple effects that came from it and the way that they impacted me, my career, my family, and my son."

schema.headline: They lost their jobs after posting about Charlie Kirk, but some have no regrets

title: Student loan terms to be made clearer in England
description: University applicants in England will be given clearer information about student loans before they take them out, the government has said.Ministers sa
body: University applicants in England will be given clearer information about student loans before they take them out, the government has said.Ministers said they would spell out that governments can change repayment rules and that different career choices can affect how much borrowers repay.They agreed to some but not all of the recommendations made by MPs after an inquiry into student loans, and did not say whether they would reverse a freeze to the repayment threshold for some graduates.The inquiry found the way loans had been presented to teenagers amounted to mis-selling, after the BBC revealed the Department for Education (DfE) had compared repayments to £30-a-month phone contracts.The recent debate has centred around Plan 2 loans, which were issued in England between September 2012 and July 2023, and are still issued in Wales.The interest rate on those loans is the Retail Prices Index (RPI) measure of inflation plus up to 3% depending on earnings, and borrowers repay at a rate of 9% of everything they earn over a repayment threshold, which is meant to rise with inflation every year. The loans are written off after 30 years.Campaigners want a lower interest rate, a lower repayment rate and for the government to reverse a decision last year to freeze the threshold at £29,385 for three years in England.Freezing that threshold means graduates start repaying their loans sooner and, once they do, they pay more than they would have done if it had risen with inflation.MPs on the Treasury Committee called for a U-turn on that decision as part of a series of recommendations after an inquiry this summer.The Treasury and the DfE did not say whether ministers would unfreeze the threshold in their response, but said: "We keep all aspects of the student finance system under review."The government rejected recommendations to:Split the cost of university evenly between the student and the governmentStop using RPI to calculate interest ratesEnsure promotional materials comply with Financial Conduct Authority's Consumer Duty, saying student loans were "very different to commercial loans"Students starting university in England now have Plan 5 loans, which have a lower interest rate but also a lower threshold and longer repayment term.Nick Hillman, director of the Higher Education Policy Institute, who helped design the Plan 2 system, said the government had "absolutely rejected" most of what the Treasury Committee had recommended and its response would not meet the concerns of Plan 2 graduates.Oliver Gardner, founder of the Rethink Repayment campaign, said the government's response "does not go far enough" and he wanted to see "concrete action" in the autumn Budget.While Dame Meg Hillier, chair of the Treasury Committee, said making information clearer was "an important step" but "doesn't help graduates who are angry that they didn't receive the same service and are now facing punitive repayment terms on a loan which keeps growing".She urged the chancellor to reverse the threshold freeze in this autumn's Budget. In March, a BBC investigation found that as well as comparing monthly student loan repayments to phone contracts, the government told presenters to "avoid words [or] phrases like debt" during presentations in schools across England a decade ago.More than 120 MPs and peers recently signed a letter coordinated by the campaign group Rethink Repayment calling for an "urgent review" of the system.One of the signatories, Liberal Democrat MP Tom Gordon, who is a Plan 2 borrower, is set to introduce a bill calling for a review in Parliament next week.Education Secretary Lucy Powell has previously said the interest rate on Plan 2 loans was "egregious" and the issue was at the top of her in-tray.The Student Loans Company said it was working with the government to "provide clear, relatable and trusted guidance".

schema.headline: Student loan terms to be made clearer in England

title: Major fire breaks out again at arson-hit Dalton Mills in Keighley
description: Major fire at derelict Peaky Blinders mill  Image source, Gazz HallImage caption, The massive blaze broke out at Dalton Mills at about 20:00 BST on Sa
body: Major fire at derelict Peaky Blinders mill  Image source, Gazz HallImage caption, The massive blaze broke out at Dalton Mills at about 20:00 BST on SaturdayByHayley CoyleYorkshireAnother major fire has broken out at a derelict mill complex where Peaky Blinders was filmed. The blaze at Dalton Mills in Keighley started at about 20:00 BST on Saturday and at its peak required 12 fire engines to tackle it. West Yorkshire Fire and Rescue Service (WYFRS) confirmed that due to the severity of the incident a number of nearby residents were evacuated and at 23:00 BST, 10 fire engines were still in attendance. A spokesperson added: "Members of the public are still advised to avoid the area to allow emergency services to operate safely and effectively." Image source, Gazz HallImage caption, At its height the blaze needed 12 crews, said WYFRS Bradford Council emergency planning officers were also at the scene to provide "support and guidance" to those affected by the evacuation.It is the third fire this year at the Grade II-listed Victorian building, which was used as a filming location for period dramas Peaky Blinders and Downton Abbey.Crews were also called to a blaze there in July 2025 and there was a major fire that destroyed a significant part of the former textile mill in 2022.  Police previously said they believed most of the fires to be deliberate and two teenagers were convicted of arson in relation to the 2022 incident.  Robbie Moore, MP for Keighley & Ilkley, said the fire was "extremely concerning". Image source, Gazz HallImage caption, The mill has been a target for arson in the past He said in a video posted on X: "It is deeply infuriating. "This situation simply cannot continue. I have been calling on our local authority to secure this site as best as possible for years now." He also thanked WYFRS and police for being "incredibly efficient" and said he was in contact with local residents who were concerned about the embers and other issues.A WYFRS spokesperson added: "Please avoid the area while emergency crews work at the scene and residents nearby are advised to keep their windows and doors closed until further notice." In 2024 the Crown Estate took legal responsibility for the building under ancient property laws after the last owner gave up his rights to it when he went bankrupt and a restoration project collapsed.Bradford Council has previously said that the Crown Estate is aware of security concerns around the abandoned site, which has suffered from repeated trespass incidents.The council said it was working with Historic England on additional security measures.Get in touchYour Voice

title: Some dentists say more young people are grinding their teeth - are you one of them?
description: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Nearly one in four people are thought to have bruxism, although most are unaware they grind their teethByRuth
body: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Nearly one in four people are thought to have bruxism, although most are unaware they grind their teethByRuth CleggHealth and wellbeing reporterUpdated 9 hours agoElla can't remember when she first started grinding her teeth at night, but she can vividly recall the excruciating jaw ache, the headaches, and being told her molars were disappearing."I was in so much pain," Ella says. "My face was changing shape and my teeth were at risk of breaking - I knew I had to do something about it."The 31-year-old has bruxism, a condition which can cause regular and often intense teeth grinding, but says the treatment she's recently had has "without a doubt" changed her life.Bruxism affects millions like Ella across the UK, external. Some studies suggest nearly one in four people experience the condition, although many may be unaware until symptoms appear.According to the British Dental Association there is some anecdotal evidence that bruxism is becoming more common, but no specific figures. However, some dentists have told the BBC they are worried about the increasing number of young people they're seeing with dental problems caused by incessant gnashing."It is definitely on the rise," Dr Aditi Desai, president of the British Society of Dental Sleep Medicine (BSDSM), says. "And it's no surprise given that life itself nowadays can be so stressful."Image source, EllaImage caption, Ella says constant teeth grinding enlarged her masseter muscles and widened her jaw (pictured, left, before treatment and, right, afterwards)Studies, external suggest many of us Bruxers do it because of stress - but why do our jaws carry the burden of our everyday lives? What can we do about it? And can it actually be a good thing in some cases?Bruxism is an umbrella term which groups together four different jaw movements - clenching, grinding, bracing and thrusting.Some people grind at night, others through the day. Some barely notice they're doing it, while others can gnash through mouthguards and wake even the deepest sleeping bed partners. So how can you tell if you do it? Here are the signs to look out for: Worn, chipped or flattened teethHeadaches or facial pain in the morningJaw stiffnessDisrupted sleep and daytime tirednessIncreased tooth sensitivityEarache or pain near the temples without infectionTeeth grinding is also mentioned more frequently in therapy according to the British Association for Counselling and Psychotherapy, which says people nowadays are more aware of how their mental health impacts their body.Psychotherapist Rahi Popat says more of his clients - particularly younger ones - say they or someone else have noticed they've been grinding their teeth, "and they can often link that to a really stressful time in their lives and realise that's when their teeth grinding either increased or even started".'A way of releasing some of the stress' Trauma and stress can put you in "fight or flight" mode, where your heart rate increases, you release adrenaline, and your muscles tense, preparing the body for an external threat, he says. And because the jaw and the nervous system are so closely linked through the major cranial nerves, our muscles are triggered and we clench and grind our teeth."If we do it overnight, it's a way of our bodies releasing some of the stress and tension we might have felt through the day," Popat explains.For Ella, nocturnal teeth grinding in her sleep became a way to release tension that had built up while she was awake. "I know it's to do with my stress levels," Ella says. "I have high functioning anxiety - you wouldn't think it if you met me."I'm busy, and I go out a lot to mask it."In her 20s, she says she just "put up" with the pain. But a few years later, when her dentist told her that her teeth were at risk, Ella decided to get treatment.Image source, EllaImage caption, After her dentist injected her jaw muscles with Botox, Ella says her sleep and mental health improvedEven though it's not routinely offered on the NHS, Ella decided to pay her dentist to inject Botox into her masseter muscles - the ones that control her jaw. The procedure relaxed them and reduced the tension in her face, and should last 3 to 4 months."Over the past few months I've been able to sleep properly," she says. "I've got so much more energy in the mornings, the pain has reduced and my face is not as square."Dr Simon Cove, a dentist who treats both private and NHS patients, says the physical impact of grinding on our teeth can be huge.He uses a 3D scanner to assess his patients' teeth, and can see the wear over time."Often people are not even aware they are doing it, but then we get to see the damage," he says. "If the teeth have been worn down to such an extent, treatment can be extremely complex and can cost thousands of pounds."But he says such cases are relatively uncommon and can take years to develop.Image source, Simon CoveImage caption, A 3D scan can reveal the damage that teeth grinders are doing to their teethWhile you can treat the symptoms - by wearing a mouthguard, for example - getting to the source of what's causing your teeth grinding is just as important, says dental sleep specialist, Dr Aditi Desai."Too often," she says, "dentists give out mouthguards without checking why it is happening."It's vital that serious, underlying conditions like obstructive sleep apnoea (OSA) are considered, she says. OSA is caused by a blocked airway, so a patient may grind their teeth to move the blockage in order to be able to breathe again."That's a very good example of why bruxism can keep you alive," says Prof Frank Lobbezoo, a leading researcher on the condition.And even though bruxism has its negatives (tooth damage, sleep disruption, jaw ache, to name but a few), it's not always the "bad guy", he explains."Bruxism is also important for the production of saliva," Lobbezoo says. "Moving the jaw muscles activates the big salivary glands. It cleans the mouth, it protects the teeth and it's vital for digestion." Some studies also suggest that chewing can help with cognition."We know this in animals, and our preliminary research is showing it in humans," he says. "By working our jaw muscles we are stimulating blood flow to the brain."But teeth grinding can also cause chronic pain, which can have a huge impact on your daily life.What is the treatment for bruxism? Dentist Riaz Yar, a specialist in prosthodontics, treats patients struggling with the effects of severe bruxism - worn, cracked and fractured teeth, and dental work that keeps failing. Many also arrive with chronic jaw or facial pain and report poor sleep, all of which need assessing in their own right, he says, rather than simply being blamed on the grinding.In the past, Yar says, teeth grinding was considered simply a mechanical problem of the jaw, but now there is strong evidence that it is much more complex. It's a "biopsychosocial issue", he says, driven by the brain and nervous system and shaped by the whole person."We take into account their sleep patterns, their diet, their weight, the amount they exercise, what medication they might be taking and we assess for signs of sleep disorders," he says. "Many factors can contribute to a patient grinding their teeth, so addressing the condition requires a multidisciplinary approach." How best to tackle it? These things might help: Mouthguard to wear at night to protect your teethIf linked to sleep apnoea, devices such as a CPAP machine or a mandibular advancement device (MAD) to help keep the airway openPhysiotherapyTalking therapies such as CBTLifestyle changes to help reduce stress and improve sleep such as exercise, cutting down on alcohol, stopping smoking and eating healthierFor severe cases Botox is an option, but it's rarely available on the NHSAlong with muscle-relaxing injections, Ella says she is also meditating to try to reduce her anxiety and free herself from the tension she regularly carries."Having treatment has transformed my life," Ella says, "now I want to try and figure out the root cause."Get in touchHave you been affected by the issues discussed in this story?

title: Why some women are 'cycle-syncing' their workouts
description: Menstrual fitness: Why some women are 'cycle-syncing' their workoutsImage source, Sarah MackayImage caption, Sarah Mackay, known as @fitwsarah online,
body: Menstrual fitness: Why some women are 'cycle-syncing' their workoutsImage source, Sarah MackayImage caption, Sarah Mackay, known as @fitwsarah online, says her energy levels change through her cycleByZara SalariaBBC NewsA woman points to a colour-coded grid dividing the menstrual cycle into four phases, each paired with a different list of exercises."When you're bleeding, you want to be doing steady-pace jogging, Pilates, barre, walking, resting," she tells viewers.This is one of thousands of videos on TikTok and Instagram suggesting that people change their workouts depending on where they are in their menstrual cycles - something known as 'cycle-syncing'.So-called cycle-syncing workout plans have surged in popularity online, with Google searches for the term rising 740% since 2022 and more than 55,000 TikTok videos now using the #cyclesyncing hashtag.Most of the advice is shared by fitness and wellness creators rather than medical or research experts.They divide the menstrual cycle into phases, recommending: gentler exercise during menstruationgradually increasing intensity in the follicular phase leading up to ovulationharder strength or high-intensity training around ovulationeasing off again during the luteal phase (between ovulation and the start of your period)So what does the science say?'A trend based on marketing'Kelly McNulty, a researcher at Leeds Beckett University specialising in menstrual cycles and exercise, says there is evidence that some women experience changes in symptoms, energy or perceived strength across their cycle.But that is different from evidence that all women should train in a particular way at a particular point, she tells the BBC, adding that these videos are "a trend based on marketing rather than any kind of research or evidence"."There isn't any research to support that kind of phase-based prescription," she says.Figure caption, Should you sync your exercise routine with your period?A key issue is that menstrual cycles are highly individual, McNulty adds - they can differ between women, and one woman's experience can also change from one cycle to the next.That makes the blanket advice often found on social media difficult to apply, she explains.Many cycle-tracking apps and programmes are also designed around relatively regular menstrual cycles that are 21 to 35 days, which can make their recommendations less applicable to people with irregular periods, or those using hormonal contraception."It's not so much about doing certain exercises in certain phases, it's about working with your own individual body and what your needs might be."Image caption, There are now thousands of videos on Instagram and TikTok recommending women sync their workouts to their menstrual cyclesIntuitive changes rather than strict plansCesci Burgoyne, a nurse based in Sydney, Australia who is also a qualified personal trainer and nutritionist, adjusts her training depending on how she feels in her cycle. She doesn't follow a prescriptive plan, she says, but instead makes changes intuitively."In my luteal phase I'll try and ease off in the training," she tells the BBC. "In my follicular phase, I'm so energised, I feel like I can lift so much heavier. I like to try and get my long runs in."Burgoyne also welcomes the growing attention on women's health, and says that exercise and nutrition research has historically focused heavily on male bodies, with findings then often applied to women.Image source, Sarah MackayImage caption, Sarah says she has sometimes hit personal records while on her periodFitness creator Sarah Mackay, known as @liftwsarah on Instagram and TikTok, has also noticed her energy, motivation, cramps and mood change through the month.But she deliberately avoids strict plans because, she says, "there are too many variables at play".Some online plans advise women to avoid intense training during their period, she says, yet she has sometimes hit personal records while menstruating."The problem is not that the menstrual cycle is irrelevant," she says, but that "not everything is predictable".The 'nocebo' effectDr Faye Bate, a trained medical doctor and women's health expert, is also wary of advice suggesting all women should train differently according to their menstrual phase."A one-size-fits-all model of 'you should be exercising this way in this phase and a different way in a different phase' shouldn't be advice that applies to all women," she says.She is concerned that repeatedly telling women they are likely to be weaker or less capable at particular points in their cycle could create a "nocebo" effect - where negative expectations themselves influence how someone feels or performs.McNulty tells the BBC that routinely easing off resistance training could also limit progress. Strength training is particularly important for women, who face a higher risk of osteoporosis later in life. Building strength requires consistent, progressively challenging training, she says, and "we don't want to create another barrier by suggesting women train less for almost half the month."Dr Bate also warns against normalising severe symptoms: if pain, fatigue or mood changes interfere with exercise or daily life, women should seek medical advice rather than assuming it is an inevitable part of their cycle, she says.How to be 'cycle-aware'While cycle-syncing itself may not be backed by strong evidence, the experts we spoke to did suggest being "cycle-aware".McNulty says tracking your cycle can be a useful way to understand your own patterns, while Dr Bate also encourages women to become more familiar with how they feel at different points in the month. Both welcome the fact that menstrual health is being discussed more openly, but say the focus should be on individual experience, rather than rigid, phase-based rules.In practice, that might mean having painkillers ready before your period, taking a rest day when symptoms are worse, or easing off a workout if you feel unusually fatigued.For Dr Bate, "the most important part is tuning in to how you feel".In other words, use your cycle as information rather than a set of rules.Get our flagship newsletter with all the headlines you need to start the day. Sign up here.
