title: Conor Benn: Two-round defeat by Ryan Garcia in Las Vegas shows British fighter's limitations
description: On one side of the road, Las Vegas tourists were being turned upside down on the New York-New York Hotel's rollercoaster.On the other side, the bigges
body: On one side of the road, Las Vegas tourists were being turned upside down on the New York-New York Hotel's rollercoaster.On the other side, the biggest night of Conor Benn's career plummeted into freefall.The polarising British welterweight arrived at T-Mobile Arena chasing a first world title and vindication after four chaotic years that stretched his reputation, career and resolve almost to breaking point.But rather than Benn leaving with his mission accomplished, Ryan Garcia laid bare the unforgiving reality of elite-level boxing, taking just two rounds to dismantle, drop and stop the 29-year-old.The Essex fighter's career has been so consumed by events outside the ring - the failed drugs test and provisional suspension, the WBC's mocked "highly elevated egg consumption" ruling, the Chris Eubank Jr saga and an acrimonious split with Eddie Hearn - that the most basic question of just how good he actually is had become obscured."It went kind of exactly how I imagined it. He was going to try and put pressure on me straight away," Garcia said afterwards."He was banking on the idea I may just start folding early on and maybe get tired. You can't jump in like that. It's not the move."Benn was taken to hospital after the fight, in what was understood to be a precautionary measure.The manner of defeat provided the clearest answer yet about Benn's place in the boxing world order.It forces a reassessment of the route which brought Benn here, and whether his body of work really suggested he was ready for, or deserving of, a world-title fight.Thirty-six years after Nigel Benn stopped Iran Barkley in the opening round in Las Vegas, his son was chasing his own defining night.As the Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua era moves towards its conclusion, British boxing is increasingly searching for its next crossover star and Benn looked the part in Las Vegas before battle commenced.He had the swagger, the looks and the tailor-made dress sense. Speaking Spanish during media interviews even helped turn some Mexican boos into cheers.The Americans bought into the package and Zuffa Boxing leaned heavily into his aura, with Dame Helen Mirren narrating a promotional film charting his rise.But looking like a world-level star and possessing world-level ability are not the same thing.Benn entered as the WBC's number one contender and BoxRec's highest-ranked British welterweight despite his inactivity in the division.British boxing has now been given two uncomfortable reminders about 'levels' in quick succession.Nobody should begrudge a fighter for accepting a life-changing world-title shot, but bypassing the traditional British, Commonwealth and European route removes learning fights.Heavyweight Moses Itauma has extraordinary talent but was accelerated towards a world title fight with Filip Hrgovic before his professional education had fully caught up.Benn's route was different, and Itauma was winning his own showpiece fight last month before being stopped, but the lesson is strikingly similar."I think he needs a little bit more patience," Garcia said - almost identical advice to that offered by Hrgovic to Itauma.Some might argue that 'burst' is too final.It would be unfair not to credit Benn's in-ring evolution, going from a raw novice who used to take beatings in sparring to becoming one of British boxing's most recognisable fighters.There will still be major fights available, not least a potential trilogy with Eubank.But his next decision now carries greater significance.Benn had said he planned to move up in weight regardless of Saturday's result.With no rehydration clause, he looked strikingly bigger in the ring and had posted footage on Friday evening suggesting he was 32lb heavier than at the official weigh-in, although the figure was not independently verified.That inevitably reignites debate around extreme weight cutting, but there is also a more immediate sporting concern. If Benn struggled so badly with Garcia's speed and timing, moving up to face naturally bigger men brings its own dangers.Zuffa Boxing chief Dana White largely sidestepped that question afterwards."Let Conor go home, spend some time with his family, enjoy the success he had this year," White said. "When he's ready to come back and lets us know, we'll figure out what's next for him."Asked whether moving up against bigger opponents could prove even more dangerous, White said: "We'll see. We'll see how the whole thing figures out."Benn did not attend the post-fight news conference, leaving White to face questions about a fighter Zuffa reportedly paid £11m to sign for his initial deal.Asked whether Benn had still been worth the money, White bluntly said: "Every penny of it."But after Garcia exposed such a sizeable gulf, the road to becoming a world champion suddenly looks considerably longer than it did when he arrived in Las Vegas.

schema.headline: Conor Benn: Two-round defeat by Ryan Garcia in Las Vegas shows British fighter's limitations

title: Will the Thirlwall report change the debate about Lucy Letby?
description: The quick take is this. The report won't change the narrative about Letby's guilt or innocence because it didn't examine that subject at all. That was
body: The quick take is this. The report won't change the narrative about Letby's guilt or innocence because it didn't examine that subject at all. That wasn't its remit.Lady Justice Thirlwall said she had "approached the inquiry on the basis that Lucy Letby is guilty of the crimes of which she has been convicted".She emphasised that it was not her role "to set about reviewing the convictions", telling the inquiry: "The Court of Appeal has done that, with a very clear result."But there is also a longer, more complex answer.Whatever the report's conclusions, Letby's convictions will stand. However, the inquiry hasn't operated in a vacuum. There are other parts of the legal system which will have an eye on its findings.And the chairwoman of the Criminal Cases Review Commission (CCRC) - the only organisation with the power to send Letby's case back to the Court of Appeal - has told the BBC the CCRC will be paying close attention to Thirlwall.Dame Vera Baird said: "We will be looking at the report with interest to assess whether it has any bearing on our review of the case."The CCRC has given no indication of when it will make its decision.But while questions over Letby's convictions weren't within the scope of the Thirlwall Inquiry, it didn't stop the subject making itself felt within the hearing room.Just as the inquiry was wrapping up, the hospital's former executives applied for it to be delayed until the CCRC has made its decision.Letters pushing for a delay were also written to the inquiry by Letby's lawyers and Sir David Davis, an MP who has campaigned on her behalf.Sir David argued that an inquiry "predicated on the presumption that Lucy Letby's conviction is safe, when there is now a wealth of authoritative voices questioning that conviction, will only undermine the conclusions arrived at by your inquiry and potentially lead to more babies dying unnecessarily".Lady Justice Thirlwall refused the requests to pause the inquiry. She said that she was not scrutinising Letby's actions, but those of the officials and managers who were responsible for responding to the crisis.The most stark question it may answer is whether any babies might have lived, or avoided injury, if action had been taken earlier.The inquiry released thousands of documents which shed new light on what was going on inside the hospital. When the hearings finished, we put together this timeline which illustrates how events unfolded.Should alarm bells have started ringing as early as June 2015 when three babies died in quick succession – the same number of deaths within two weeks that the unit would normally expect in a year? What about in August 2015, when a baby was poisoned with insulin?The results of his blood test didn't raise an alert. At the inquiry, hospital consultants accepted this had been a "collective failure".Lawyers for the baby's family said the test results "provided the clearest opportunity to detect and stop Letby" and were "a bright line within the chronology after which no babies should have been harmed".By early 2016, senior managers including medical director Ian Harvey and director of nursing Alison Kelly knew there was an unusually high death rate on the neonatal unit and that there were escalating concerns about a nurse. But it didn't lead to safeguarding action.It was only after two triplet brothers died in June 2016 that Letby was taken off nursing duty.Dr Rosie Benneyworth, who gave evidence to the inquiry, also believes the report has the potential to make a difference across the NHS."We can't keep going on diagnosing the problem, and not making the change," said Benneyworth, who is chief executive of the Health Services Safety Investigations Body.She said the inquiry had "a huge amount" to report on and that it needed to lead to cultural change to help keep patients safe.Carla Duprey of Bond Turner solicitors, who represents two families at the inquiry, sees the length of time taken to produce the report as a positive sign that Lady Justice Thirlwall has left no stone unturned."I am optimistic that the report is going to be thorough, will raise criticisms, and will hopefully result in some real change," she said.And then there is the public debate.As the legal wheels have been turning in the background, those campaigning to free Letby have redoubled their efforts, with protests and websites dedicated to her cause. But there are also strong feelings from those who believe she belongs in jail. Both sides have found energy online, within highly active forums on Facebook, Reddit, Tattle Life, and elsewhere.How will Lady Justice Thirlwall's report go down with those communities?David Wilson, emeritus professor of criminology at Birmingham City University, believes it's unlikely that the report will reverse hard-baked opinions."The 'noisier' Letby commentators are almost universally on the side that she is innocent," he says. "I have no doubt there will be aspects of the governance of the hospital where she killed within the report that will be harnessed to support that view."Prof Wilson believes it will become "another component of the information war that's constantly being waged about her guilt or innocence" and he feels much of the conversation about Letby "seems to generate more heat than light".One thing is certain. No matter what their point of view, everyone with a strong opinion about Letby will pay close attention to the report. Even those who wanted it to be delayed, or who didn't support it in the first place, will scour its findings.But it's much less likely to take the heat out of the public debate or draw a line under the case. Those who say they're already sure about Lucy Letby may scrutinise the report, but take from it whatever supports those ready-formed views.

schema.headline: Will the Thirlwall report change the debate about Lucy Letby?

title: Swansea man who 'should be dead' reunites with teacher who changed his life
description: I should be dead or in prison - now I'm reunited with the teacher who changed my lifeFigure caption, I'm reunited with the teacher who changed my life
body: I should be dead or in prison - now I'm reunited with the teacher who changed my lifeFigure caption, I'm reunited with the teacher who changed my lifeByGemma DunstanBBC WalesUpdated 9 September 2026"Statistically I should be dead, in prison or homeless."Sam Gardner lived in 15 foster homes between the ages of three and 17, and said the instability was a "big challenge". He never felt at home anywhere and was sometimes hungry and neglected. When he left the care system at 18, his future was uncertain.But he said a few "anchors" helped him to lay the foundations for adulthood. Now, the BBC has helped to reunite the 33-year-old with one of them - his former teacher who "saw past" Sam being a child in foster care."She made me feel like I belonged," said Sam, who went on to become a teacher himself.Image caption, Twenty-five years after she taught him in primary school, Ms Meek and Sam met again Sam said he didn't really feel at home until he met his last set of foster carers, when he was aged 17.Despite his start in life, Sam defied the odds to become a primary school teacher, inspired by one special woman who he said believed in him at his school in south Wales."She wasn't a perfect teacher but she saw past my label as a looked-after child. She also demanded that I didn't look at that label," recalled Sam.He said before joining Christine Meek's class aged eight, school was a "challenging place" and that he was academically two years behind his peers.Sam's story of hope comes after a recent report found young care leavers in England are dying at a far higher rate than other people their age.Image source, Sam GardnerImage caption, Sam entered the care system aged three and went to several schoolsBBC Wales reunited Ms Meek and Sam at St Michael's Catholic Primary School in Pontypridd, where she first taught him 25 years ago."I just want to say you've changed my life, I wouldn't be where I am without you," said Sam, as he hugged Ms Meek.She replied: "It's you who should be proud of what you've done, because it's you who has done it."Ms Meek described Sam as "quiet" in school "but that he also tested boundaries"."I didn't know a lot about Sam's background and in some ways I think that helps," she said."The expectations were the same for everyone in the class."Ms Meek said it was a pleasure to hear what Sam had gone on to achieve in his life."As a teacher you plant seeds, you don't know what they're going to grow and that's a lovely thing," she added.Image caption, Sam was so inspired by his old teacher Ms Meek that he went on to become a teacher himselfSam said: "Walking back through those doors as the person I am today, I realised just how much of St Michael's I'd carried with me."My childhood involved so much change, but that school gave me something steady to stand on."He said it was emotional being back, and a privilege to catch up with Ms Meek."Ms Meek and the other adults there planted seeds in me that I probably couldn't see at the time, but they became part of the foundation I grew from," he said.Sam, who now lives in Swansea, has recently been looking through his care files and shared an excerpt with the BBC.Figure caption, Twenty-five years on, Sam has the chance to thank his teacher for changing his life"Sadly there has been a great deterioration in Sam's behaviour at school and he is the cause of much concern," one read. "His class teacher is emotionally drained. He is disruptive, erratic and volatile."Sam said it had been "overwhelming" reading about his childhood in the files.With Ms Meek as his teacher, Sam was able to improve and meet school grade expectations."I was able to believe in myself because of the foundation she created," he recalled.Image source, Sam GardnerImage caption, Sam on his final day of primary school. His care files say he was upset to leave "She made me feel like I belonged and because of that I was able to achieve my potential."Sam said he had more than 50 professionals in his life, and having "anchors" who supported him was vital.It is estimated there are currently around 7,000 children in foster care in Wales and 54,000 in England, according to government data.A UK government-commissioned review found, external young care leavers in England were dying at a far higher rate than other people their age, with the report co-author calling the deaths "a national tragedy"."The corporate parent is meant to be your parent," said Sam. "What kind of parent allows that to happen to their children? We need to wake up."The hardest part of being in foster care is the transitions, moving from home to home, often with your stuff in black bags."It signals that you're different, that you don't belong, you're not valued."Image caption, Christine Meek said she didn't know much about Sam's background in foster care Sam's reunion comes after Foster Wales launched a pilot across 37 schools in Swansea and Neath Port Talbot in May, with the aim of connecting local authority fostering services directly with schools."We talk a lot about the power of one caring adult in a child's life, and that could be a teacher or member of staff within the school," said Alistair Cope, head of Foster Wales."It's been fantastic to see Sam sharing the importance of that, he's a phenomenal individual for telling his story."It is hoped the pilot will improve the support offered to children in care, so they can thrive in an educational environment.Sketty Primary School in Swansea is one of those taking part in the pilot. "We are lucky to have such strong networks of care and support around our children - and this initiative helps shine a light on that," said headteacher Simon Lloyd-Jones."It also highlights the way schools go above and beyond to support some of our most vulnerable learners, including looked-after children, helping them feel safe, valued and able to thrive."Image caption, Alistair Cope of Foster Wales says it is "massively important" that foster children have supportive people around themSam left teaching last year to work as a keynote speaker and trainer drawing on his lived experiences.He said it was his role to "speak up in rooms for children who can't always speak up for themselves"."My role isn't to call foster carers out, call the system out on what they've done wrong and how it's affected me and my life."It's more to show the impact we can have on thousands of children in this country," said Sam."Children in care experience instability on another level, and that's often misunderstood, so the more we can understand the better we can provide the support they need."The Welsh government said it "recognises the concerns raised" by people who have been in care."Sustained support for care leavers is vital, particularly as they transition into adulthood," their statement added.If you or someone you know has been affected by the issues raised in this story, information about available help and support can be found via BBC Action Line.Get in touchHave you been affected by issues raised in this story?

schema.headline: Swansea man who 'should be dead' reunites with teacher who changed his life
